body.text: United States President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin met on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.

This was the first formal trilateral meeting involving the leaders of the United States, China and Russia. The meeting reportedly lasted more than an hour, and the leaders of the three most powerful nations discussed issues related to nuclear weapons, the international order, United Nations reforms and issues relating to wider international security.
The meeting comes at a very important juncture in global politics.

Following the summit, the three countries released a joint official statement titled the “U.S.-Russia-China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace.” The joint statement outlined four primary areas of consensus, covering U.N. reform, expanded refined petroleum supply, state official immunity from International Criminal Court jurisdiction, and nuclear risk reduction dialogue.

Pakistan, like several other countries, watched the trilateral meeting closely to see what the dialogue among the three powers could mean for its own strategic interests and how it might affect the country.

For Islamabad, the Shenzhen declaration’s affirmation that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” is the summit’s most consequential takeaway. It is important to note that following the India-Pakistan military clashes in May last year, which also triggered intense international speculation and commentary over risks of nuclear escalation, Pakistani officials have repeatedly stressed that nuclear deterrence leaves zero room for war in South Asia.

Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director-general of the Inter‑Services Public Relations (ISPR), had underscored this posture in media interviews. He stated that “seeking military space or conflict space with an established nuclear power for elusive objectives is absurd, sheer stupidity, and inconceivable.” The ISPR is the media and public relations wing of the Pakistan Armed Forces.

Last month, Lt. Gen. (retired) Mazhar Jamil, an adviser to Pakistan’s National Command Authority, warned that India may be moving toward an offensive nuclear first-strike posture which, according to him, has raised the risk of a catastrophic confrontation between the two South Asian rivals. Jamil warned that the May 2025 fighting had made future crises more dangerous by narrowing the space between military action and escalation.

In this context, Pakistan will likely view the consensus reached among the U.S., China, and Russia on nuclear risk reduction and non-use in any crisis as a welcome validation of its own warnings over the dangers of confrontation between nuclear-armed states, including India and Pakistan.

Moreover, for Pakistan, it also serves as a stabilizing restraint amid media reports that the U.S. might consider tactical nuclear options in its war against neighboring Iran. Arguably, by reinforcing the global taboo against nuclear use, the trilateral agreement over the non-use of nuclear weapons strengthens Islamabad’s own diplomatic push to deter any idea of regional miscalculation with India, which might pose the danger of a nuclear spillover in any form.

The second key takeaway for Islamabad is the three countries’ commitment to pursuing United Nations reforms so the body “can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security.” Historically, Pakistan has opposed the push by the Group of Four bloc, which includes India, Brazil, Germany and Japan, for permanent membership of the U.N. Security Council. Instead, it has advocated for expansion of the elected non-permanent category to make the 15-member body more representative and effective.

During a U.N. debate in October 2026, Pakistani diplomat Ambassador Usman Jadoon encapsulated this stance, stating that Pakistan opposes the “creation of additional individual permanent seats.” “An expansion of the elected, non-permanent category, based on fair rotation through regular elections, can provide a more democratic and inclusive path forward,” he added.

Strategically, Islamabad aims to prevent regional rivals from gaining permanent Council status. In part, this is driven by Pakistan’s motivation to ensure that the United Nations plays an active role in resolving long-standing disputes like Kashmir with India. Moving forward, Pakistan will likely use the U.S.-China-Russia consensus to bolster its diplomatic push for a consensus-driven global governance at the U.N. where its interests are protected.
Overall, the trilateral meeting has been welcomed in Pakistan, which, like many other countries in the West Asia region, benefits from stability in ties between the U.S., China and Russia,

For instance, the idea of deeper cooperation among these countries could potentially result in the end of the Ukraine war, and a resolution of the crisis between Iran and the U.S., which in turn, could bring down oil prices.

Moreover, this could also create more space for middle powers like Pakistan to navigate great power competition without being forced into any form of rigid alignment. A sustained dialogue among Washington, Beijing and Moscow has the potential to ease some of the systemic pressures that smaller states routinely face.
In this regard, policymakers in Pakistan are likely to closely monitor whether the Shenzhen declaration translates into concrete follow-up steps.
